transcript:
[00:00] Ava (Redwood): Hey everyone, welcome to the Redwood customer podcast. happy to have BrightWave here. Quick intros?
[00:10] Laura (BrightWave): hi all, Laura Martinez, Head of AI at BrightWave. we run personalization and content generation for clients. thanks for having us.
[00:18] Neil (Redwood AE): Neil Park, AE at Redwood. excited to hear your story.
[00:21] Ellen (BrightWave): Ellen Cho, CMO, nice to meet you.
[00:25] Jasmin (Redwood SE): Jasmin Malik, solutions engineer, i'll chime in on the tech bits.
[00:30] Samir (BrightWave): Samir Patel, product, handles the integrations.
[00:35] Ava: Great. So high level, Laura, can you tell us where BrightWave was before Redwood and what pushed you to change?
[00:45] Laura: Yeah so previously we were kind of on a mix of vendor endpoints and self-hosted experiments; it was messy. latency spikes during big campaigns, costs unpredictable, and the engineering work to keep things stable was heavy. we wanted something that gave us performance predictability and easier rollouts across clients.
[01:10] Neil: When you say latency spikes, what were you seeing? numbers?
[01:14] Laura: on peak loads, p95 was around 1.2s to 1.5s for our 1k token prompts which is rough for interactive editing flows. after Redwood we got to around 400-500ms p95 with dedicated pools and better batching.
[01:33] Jasmin: to add, we helped them tune batching windows and prefix caching; the KV cache was a big win even though early docs call it K-V cash in places—(laughs).
[01:43] Laura: yeah we did have some small naming issues in the proto docs, ha. but the caching cut repeated token cost a lot.
[01:50] Ellen: curious — did you consider staying with hosted endpoints from big providers instead of dedicated?
[01:56] Samir: we did the math. hosted was easier but cost per 1k tokens at scale, and the variability across regions was a problem. Redwood's dedicated pricing and the burst policies made predictable monthly costs nicer. plus the routing rules meant we could failover if a region has trouble.
[02:18] Neil: there's often a tradeoff lat vs cost. you mentioned burst capacity — did you use that much?
[02:24] Laura: during launches, yes. especially when we had a new template release across thousands of accounts; Redwood's autoscale and burst for a few hours saved us from throttling.
[02:35] Ava: let's jump to security because a lot of listeners care. what controls mattered for you?
[02:40] Laura: SOC 2 was table stakes, we also needed KMS integration for key management, and a VPC option for some regulated clients. Redwood's audit logs and SSO integration with our Okta SAML made the enterprise sales motion much easier.
[02:57] Jasmin: we also provided a private deployment option for a pilot in EU region, they wanted data residency. some of the wording in the compliance doc was tough to parse but we iterated.
[03:08] Samir: yep, the legal team dug into encryption at rest details. the HSM/KMS references were important.
[03:14] Ellen: from a marketing POV, the speed improvements translated to better demo experiences for clients — and that matters for conversion.
[03:22] Laura: and dev time saved. we spent less time firefighting inference infra and more time on prompts and evaluation.
[03:30] Neil: can you share any numbers on cost reduction?
[03:33] Laura: rough numbers: we saw about 25-30% reduction in token cost after switching quantized model variants and enabling caching for common prefixes. combined with lower ops overhead, the total TCO win was closer to 40% first year.
[03:48] Jasmin: also model selection helped — we matched tasks to smaller, faster variants where appropriate. that cut compute time.
[03:55] Samir: there was a moment where we tried to use a more expensive model for everything and the cost blew up, the Redwood team helped set routing policies so heavy workloads hit higher-capacity endpoints only when needed.
[04:09] Ava: nice. listeners always like a quick anecdote — any memorable outage or hiccup story and how Redwood helped?
[04:18] Laura: early on we had a big campaign, a 3rd-party region had a problem; Redwood's auto-fallback to another region kept the UI responsive. there were some dropped requests but overall no client impact.
[04:30] Neil: that's the graceful degradation stuff we aim for.
[04:33] Ellen: i remember that week; it was a relief.
[04:36] [04:36] Speaker 2 (transcription glitch): the the the —
[04:40] Ava: (laughs) yeah, transcription is sometimes funky.
[04:43] [05:05] Laura: on the product side, integrations were straightforward. we used the SDK and the templates in the docs. Jasmin, you helped with a plugin for our internal playground.
[05:16] Jasmin: yep. i recall we adjusted the latency SLOs per route; the console made it easier to see which prompts were hot and where to apply caching.
[05:30] Samir: On that, the token-level cost breakdown in the console is great for budgeting. marketing would check it before big campaigns.
[05:38] Ellen: guilty. (laughs)
[05:40] [06:00] Ava: switching gears — from a storytelling perspective, what surprised you most after migrating?
[06:07] Laura: the biggest surprise was developer velocity. once the infra issues were handled, our ML engineers spent weeks on prompt engineering that actually improved CTR. we didn't expect that kind of product win so fast.
[06:20] Neil: did you run evals or quality monitoring tied to prompt sets?
[06:24] Samir: yes, we set up evaluation suites and Redwood Optimize alerted on regressions when we rolled new model versions. that saved a bad rollout.
[06:34] Jasmin: quick note — model rollouts with canary + automatic fallback was something they used heavily.
[06:41] Laura: i also liked how the rollout policy allowed us to pin a model version per client. for sensitive clients we kept older models until approvals passed.
[06:52] [07:10] Ava: okay fun lightning round — favorite feature?
[07:13] Ellen: the console's token cost view.
[07:15] Samir: routing rules.
[07:17] Laura: KV caching.
[07:18] Jasmin: canary rollouts.
[07:20] Neil: (muffled) my favorite is the observability hooks.
[07:25] [08:00] Ava: this is great material for the episode. quick editing note — we'll probably trim a few technical tangents for the main cut but keep an extended version for partners. are you all comfortable with the release?
[08:12] Laura: yes, as long as we approve the final transcript and the highlight quote.
[08:17] Ellen: marketing assets too — logos, headshots.
[08:20] Ava: perfect. Any final tips for other teams thinking of moving to dedicated inference?
[08:25] Laura: start with a small pilot focused on one high-value flow, measure latency and cost per 1k tokens, and don't underestimate caching.
[08:35] Samir: involve security/legal early if you need KMS/VPC; it avoids late surprises.
[08:41] Jasmin: and run evals tied to your critical prompts — Redwood Optimize helps there.
[08:48] [10:02] Neil: quick housekeeping — we'll send a short follow-up with the draft audio and show notes.
[10:08] Ava: awesome. thanks everyone. final quick lightning thing — any competitors you looked at and why Redwood won out?
[10:16] Laura: we looked at the usual suspects — OpenAI for hosted simplicity, Anthropic for safety models, Cohere for embeddings. Redwood won on the combination of dedicated performance, cost controls, and the enterprise features (SAML, audit logs).
[10:34] Ellen: plus the team's responsiveness during the pilot was a big factor.
[10:38] [11:00] Ava: great. last question — anything you want mentioned verbatim in the case study?
[11:06] Laura: you can quote me: 'Redwood helped BrightWave reduce inference cost and double down on prompt quality — the result was faster dev cycles and better conversion on campaigns.'
[11:22] Ellen: 'The predictability in cost and latency let us run campaigns with confidence.'
[11:29] Ava: perfect. we'll send the quote for approval.
[11:33] [12:00] (conversation winds down; casual signoffs)
[12:10] Samir: Thanks everyone, excited to see the cut.
[12:14] Neil: Thanks BrightWave, appreciate you joining.
[12:17] Laura: Thanks all.
[12:20] Ava: Bye!
